newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-GROBBELAAR PICKED UP CASH FOR RIGGING GAME - CLAIM.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GROBBELAAR PICKED UP CASH FOR RIGGING GAME - CLAIM.

text.p: Former Liverpool soccer star Bruce Grobbelaar, unhappy about his wages, was paid 40,000 pounds ($67,000) in 1993 for rigging a match to benefit a Far Eastern betting syndicate, a court heart on Tuesday.

Grobbelaar -- who won five league titles with Liverpool -- and three other defendants were appearing in the southern town of Winchester on the first day of their trial on match-rigging charges, the first of its kind in Britain for 30 years.

Prosecutor David Calvert Smith, outlining the case against Grobbelaar, said the 39-year-old Zimbabwean-born player offered to fix matches after becoming embittered that other team-mates at Liverpool were receiving more money than him.
Calvert Smith said main prosecution witness Chris Vincent would relate how Grobbelaar said the syndicate was prepared to pay "big bucks" to throw a game, up to 40,000 pounds.
"Vincent says that some time late in November 1993 Grobbelaar told him he `would do the business' that weekend," Calvert Smith said.
On November 20, with Grobbelaar in goal, Liverpool lost 3-0 at rivals Newcastle.
"Shortly after the game ended, Grobbelaar called Vincent to say it had been a good result," the prosecutor said. A few days later the two men flew down to London to pick up the money.

They drove to a luxurious north London house, where Grobbelaar -- carrying a briefcase -- was met by co-defendant John Fashanu. Shortly afterwards he emerged and told Vincent to count the money in the case, which totalled 40,000 pounds.
Calvert Smith said Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim, also on trial, had regularly received large amounts of money from Indonesia to finance the match-rigging.
He said the fourth defendant, former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers, was also paid by Lim and Fashanu to throw matches but had nothing to do with Grobbelaar.
Detailed phone logs showed that despite protestations to the contrary, it could be shown that Fashanu and Lim were in frequent contact with both Segers and Grobbelaar.
The case broke in November 1994 when the Sun newspaper, armed with accusations from Vincent, a former business partner of Grobbelaar, accused the goalkeeper of being corrupt.
Grobbelaar told the newspaper the 40,000 pounds had come from his testimonial fund.
"As they say in the pantomime, `Oh no it didn't'" said Calvert Smith, brandishing details of payments from the fund which he said proved the keeper was telling lies.

Calvert Smith said that although the jury might not have much sympathy for Vincent, who wanted to make money from the case and had only come forward after arguing with Grobbelaar, independent evidence fully backed his testimony.
According to Vincent, Grobbelaar originally agreed only to offer advice to the syndicate. But prompted by unhappiness over his wages, the keeper decided to go further.
Calvert Smith said Grobbelaar received gross pay of 160,000 pounds ($255,000) in 1990/91 and a similar amount in 1993/94, but his wages had dropped in between.
To obscure what he was doing, the keeper invented a series of code words, referring to Lim as the "Short Man" or "Bubka", apparently an ironic reference to pole vaulter Sergei Bubka.
The prosecutor said the jury might be asking itself how a keeper could guarantee the result of a match.
"Well, of course, he can't. He may not have the opportunity to do so," he said, noting that a keeper's defenders or the opposing team could foil his attempts.
"That is exactly what happened in a game between Liverpool and Manchester United in January 1994, about which you will hear a good deal," he said.
"Goalkeepers do make a mistake sometimes, so it may be that the odd deliberate mistake may escape attention," he added.
